about: CREW CARDS (Design/npc_text_encounters.md 2.1-2.8 and samples 19-24; Design/content/BRIEF.md and BRIEF_2.md), written 4 Oct 2026: the life of the boat that is not one of the four crewmen's own chains (chain_crew_1 to 4). Pay and shares, a man who wants to go home, a baptised Frisian and a Dane who keeps to Thor on one thwart, sickness and a death and what is done with the body, hunger, cold, boredom, a fight, a theft, a friendship, men teaching each other their tongues, riddles asked for sport, reading with the crew, a new hand, a man leaving, the winter ashore, and the evening song: Beowulf, one fitt an evening at sea (crew.song.fitt_01 to fitt_43, each gated on the fitt before it by text.beowulf_NN). All are stage 'crew': drawn by 'rate' per game hour (Scheduler.HourlyWeight), at sea or moored as the 'when' says. THE SEATS: the cards speak through five fixed parts, which agree with the spine's first crew (Design/content/spine.json cast.crew.*) but never use their names, so they serve every crew to 1066: 'steersman' (a baptised Frisian), 'mate' (a Saxon who speaks for the oars), 'lookout' (a young Englishman schooled by monks, who has the song by heart), 'dane' (role crewman: a Dane or Northman who keeps the old gods) and 'hand' (role sailor: the ordinary Frisian hand). Every crew actor's tongue is old_frisian, the boat's working tongue, so nothing they say is masked. Cards that need a heathen aboard ask (year < 816 or flag.crew_heathen_aboard): the first crew has one until about 815, and crew.hire.dane sets the flag after. Flags of this file begin crew_; the only shared flags set here are hy_fed_poor (a sack of wheat given in a famine port) and bk_lost (a book lost to water), as the spine's hooks for the crew name them. Each option's outcome in words is the writing entry '<label_key>.out' ('.fail' for a failed chance) in Data/writing/crew.json: the engine shows only the effects' facts today (see the report's needs). Quotations are from texts_793.json or from translations out of copyright, named in each card's note; (?) marks what was not checked.

cards.note: Pay and shares 1 (sample 20). The wage is voyage_rules.json: a quarter penny a man a day, so a penny every four days, kept on a tally; a month for four men is 30 d. 'venture_ended' and 'days_since_paid' read 0 until the crew are modelled, so a full purse and a low heart also bring the card. Hired hands paid at the venture's end: npc_text_encounters.md 1.1 (the crew's terms) (?).
cards.when: moored and (venture_ended or days_since_paid > 30 or (silver >= 60 and heart < 0.6)) and not flag.crew_pay_promised
cards.title: The reckoning
cards.intention: The cargo is sold. The mate speaks for the men: they want what the tally says they are owed.

options.label: Count it out on the thwart (30 d)
Half now, the rest at the next landing (15 d)
Open a cask of the cargo's ale tonight; silver at the next sale
Ask them to wait

memory.pay: paid the men on the day
memory.wait: asked the men to wait for their pay

cards.note: Pay and shares 2: the promise of the card before comes due at the next landing (a flag, not a scheduled card, so it never opens at sea). A man owed fourteen days may go ashore for good: voyage_rules.json leave_if_owed_days. Frisian rents were reckoned in cloaks as readily as silver (Traditiones Fuldenses c. 7, 37: Design/content/peoples/frisian.md), so cloth is honest pay.
cards.when: moored and flag.crew_pay_promised and not flag.crew_pay_just_promised
cards.title: The promise
cards.intention: You promised the men their pay at the next landing. This is it.

options.label: Pay what was promised (20 d)
Cut a bolt of the cargo's cloth among them: worth more than they are owed
Tell them there is nothing yet

memory.pay: kept his word on the men's pay
memory.none.success: broke his word on the men's pay
memory.none.failure: broke his word on the men's pay, and a man left the boat

cards.note: Pay and shares 3: a wage, a share, or a bundle of his own. The partnership of men who put goods in one keel (Norse felag) is cut on Danish and Swedish stones about 1000 and not before (Design/content/peoples/norse.md 5), so the word is said only from 1000. A hand trading a bundle of his own is the later seamen's custom of portage; for 793 it is a guess (?).
cards.when: moored and silver >= 120 and heart >= 0.5 and not flag.crew_on_shares and not flag.crew_own_bundles
cards.title: A wage or a share
cards.intention: The house is doing well. The mate asks whether the men might have a part of the venture instead of a wage.

options.label: A tenth of each season's gain, shared among them at Martinmas
Keep the wage, but each man may carry a bundle of his own to trade
A wage is a wage

memory.share: gave the men a share in the venture
memory.bundle: let each man trade a bundle of his own
memory.wage: kept the men on a wage

cards.note: Pay and shares 4: the season's end. Easter to Martinmas (11 November) is the sailing season (research_indie_and_concept.md 4.4; peoples/frisian.md 2); Saint Martin is Utrecht's saint. The autumn slaughter at Martinmas is general custom (?).
cards.when: moored and month = 11
cards.title: Martinmas
cards.intention: The sailing season is over. The men are paid for it now, or they are owed.

options.label: Pay the season out, and something over for each man (40 d)
Pay what the tally says and no more (24 d)
Ask them to carry it on the tally till Easter

memory.over: paid the season out with something over
memory.easter: owed the men their season till Easter

cards.note: Pay and shares 5: the spine's hook for the crew in thread counts_day ('the men's shares against the count's day ... the mate would rather the count went unpaid'). The debt is trade_rules.json start (480 d to the count). Sets none of the thread's db_ flags: those are the count's cards'.
cards.when: moored and debt > 0 and debt_due_days < 40 and silver >= 30
cards.title: The count's day and the men's
cards.intention: The count's day is near and the men's day is past. There is silver enough for one of them.

options.label: The men first (24 d)
The count first; the men at the next sale
Half to the men now, and keep the rest for the count (12 d)

memory.men: paid the men before the count
memory.count: paid the count before the men

cards.note: A man who wants to go home 1. The Dane's words are Havamal 36 (texts_793.json havamal_036, Bellows 1923), given whole if the promise is made. Hay and the summer on the marsh: peoples/frisian.md 2. The man is the ordinary hand, so none of the four named crewmen's wants is touched.
cards.when: not moored and storm < 0.3 and days_at_sea > 2 and not flag.crew_home_promised and not flag.crew_home_refused and not flag.crew_man_went_home
cards.title: A man looks landward
cards.intention: The hand has had word from home. He asks to be there before the autumn storms.

options.label: Give your word: home by Michaelmas
Send silver to his father by the next Frisian boat instead (8 d)
The season is short and so is the crew. After Martinmas

memory.no: would not let him go home

cards.note: A man who wants to go home 2: the promise comes due at a landing in September or October (Michaelmas is 29 September). Paid to the day: a man aboard since Easter is owed about 40 d; 10 d is what is left on his tally after his draws (?).
cards.when: moored and flag.crew_home_promised and month >= 9 and month <= 10
cards.title: Michaelmas
cards.intention: The hand reminds you of your word. A boat for his own coast lies in the harbour.

options.label: Pay him what is on his tally and put him on the other boat (10 d)
Offer him half as much again to stay till Martinmas (6 d)
Tell him the word was given in a better month

memory.go: kept his word and sent him home
memory.break.success: broke his word about going home
memory.break.failure: broke his word, and the man went in the night

cards.note: A man who wants to go home 3: the good end. He comes back in spring with a cheese (goods_793.json cheese: a wheel, 4 d; Frisian butter and cheese: peoples/frisian.md 2).
cards.when: moored and flag.crew_man_went_home and month >= 3 and month <= 5
cards.title: A man on the mooring post
cards.intention: The hand you sent home in the autumn is back, and asks for his oar.

options.label: His oar is his
Take him back, and buy his mother's cheeses for the hold (4 d)
The oar is taken

memory.take: took him back at his oar
memory.refuse: turned him away in the spring

cards.note: A man who wants to go home 4: the homecoming at Dorestad. The lookout quotes the Exeter Book's Maxims I (B) 24-29 in Benjamin Thorpe's translation (Codex Exoniensis, 1842, p. 339; Thorpe d. 1870), as given in Design/content/peoples/frisian.md 8: an English saying about a Frisian sailor's wife, in a manuscript of about 970 holding older verse. Dorestad is gone after 863 (ports_793.json).
cards.when: moored and port.id = dorestad and year < 864 and port.visits > 1
cards.title: When the vessel stands
cards.intention: Home. The men can see their own roofs from the boat, and the cargo is still aboard.

options.label: Let them go home tonight; the cargo keeps till morning
Two ashore and two aboard, turn about
Unload first

cards.note: The Frisian and the Dane 1 (sample 22; the spine's crew hooks in cross_and_grove and saxon_end). The law quoted is the Capitulatio de partibus Saxoniae c. 4 (about 782-785) in D. C. Munro's translation (Translations and Reprints from the Original Sources of European History VI.5, 1900; Munro d. 1933), softened by the Capitulare Saxonicum of 797, so the line is said only before 798. 'fast' reads 0 until the game has fast days, so March, which lies in Lent in nearly every year, also brings the card.
cards.when: (fast or month = 3) and (year < 816 or flag.crew_heathen_aboard)
cards.title: Pork in Lent
cards.intention: A fast day for three of them and not for the fourth: the Dane has meat on the fire and the steersman will not sit downwind of it.

options.label: Order the meat put away till Easter
Buy the pork off him for the stores: in salt it will keep till Easter (2 d)
Each man keeps his own custom: he eats in the bow

memory.away: had the meat put away in Lent
memory.buy: bought the Dane's pork to keep the peace
memory.each: let each man keep his own custom

cards.note: The Frisian and the Dane 2: an offering at the start of a passage. The Dane's words follow what Landnamabok says of Helgi the Lean, who 'believed in Christ, but called on Thor for sea voyages and in hard need' (LATER: written in the 12th-13th centuries of a man of about 890; our rendering from memory (?)). Saint Martin is Utrecht's patron (peoples/frisian.md 4). Sailors' offerings before a crossing are not recorded for 793 (?).
cards.when: under_way and days_at_sea < 1 and wind >= 6 and storm < 0.3 and (year < 816 or flag.crew_heathen_aboard)
cards.title: A horn of ale and a prayer
cards.intention: The land is dropping astern. The Dane wants to pour ale over the stem for his god; the steersman wants a prayer to Saint Martin.

options.label: Let him pour
The steersman says the prayer; every man uncovers his head
The sea is wide enough for a prayer and a horn of ale

memory.pour: let the Dane pour ale to his god
memory.pray: had the prayer said and no offering

cards.note: The Frisian and the Dane 3: Radbod at the font. The tale is the Vita Vulframni c. 9, written at Fontenelle (Saint-Wandrille) about 800: Radbod, king of the Frisians (d. 719), drew his foot back from the font on hearing that his forefathers were among the damned, and said he would rather be with them than with a few poor men in heaven (our rendering; a monks' tale, not history: peoples/frisian.md 4) (?).
cards.when: not moored and storm < 0.3 and hour >= 17 and (year < 816 or flag.crew_heathen_aboard)
cards.title: One foot in the water
cards.intention: The Dane tells the steersman a story about the steersman's own king. Both of them look at you.

options.label: Laugh with the Dane
Say that a king who goes to hell for the company is still in hell
Ask each of them what his own father would have said

cards.note: The Frisian and the Dane 4: the Saxon's vow. The words are the Old Saxon baptismal vow (texts_793.json saxon_vow: Vatican, Pal. lat. 577; MGH Capitularia I pp. 222-223), given whole by the first option. Death for refusing baptism: Capitulatio de partibus Saxoniae c. 8. The spine's hook: the mate 'says the vow and means half of it'. Only while men baptised under arms are of an age to row (before 830).
cards.when: not moored and storm < 0.3 and hour >= 17 and year < 830 and not text.saxon_vow
cards.title: How a Saxon is made a Christian
cards.intention: Somebody has asked the mate how he was baptised. He answers, which he does not often do.

options.label: Ask him to say all of it, slowly
Ask him whether he meant it
Leave it there

cards.note: The Frisian and the Dane 5: a squall with thunder (not a gale: the optional cards are held back under pressure, playability_and_fun.md 2.2). Thunaer is the thunder-god's name in the Saxon vow; the fifth day of the week carries his name in Old English (Thunresdaeg) and the other Germanic tongues, priests' mouths included (?). No vow is made here: the chain storm_vow has that.
cards.when: not moored and storm >= 0.3 and storm < 0.7 and (year < 816 or flag.crew_heathen_aboard)
cards.title: Thunder
cards.intention: Thunder along the coast. The Dane is glad of it and the steersman is praying with his teeth shut. Both are holding on.

options.label: Let each call on his own, as long as the sheet is held
Silence on the thwarts; the steersman gives the words
Say that even the bishop calls the fifth day by the thunderer's name

cards.note: The Frisian and the Dane 6: a period joke. Notker of Saint Gall, Gesta Karoli II.19 (about 885), tells of Northmen who came each Easter to the court of Louis the Pious (814-840) to be baptised for the white garments and gifts; one old man, given a poor shirt when the good ones ran out, said he had been washed there some twenty times and always dressed well, and that this sack was for a swineherd, not a fighting man (our rendering; A. J. Grant's translation of 1905 is free) (?). Only in Louis's years and a little after.
cards.when: not moored and storm < 0.3 and year >= 816 and year <= 845 and flag.crew_heathen_aboard
cards.title: The white shirt
cards.intention: The steersman asks the Dane, not for the first time, whether he will ever be baptised. The Dane says he has been.

options.label: Ask what became of the first two shirts
Tell him not to tell that one where a priest can hear
Ask what a white shirt of that linen fetches in the north

cards.note: The Frisian and the Dane 7: the first signing. At Sliaswic about 850 many 'were willingly signed with the cross in order that they might become catechumens', so as to enter the church and deal with Christians, and put baptism off to the end of their lives (Rimbert, Vita Anskarii c. 24, tr. C. H. Robinson 1921; our paraphrase). Egils saga's prime-signing is LATER. Only from 830, when the mission to the Danes is a generation old.
cards.when: moored and port.faith = christian and year >= 830 and flag.crew_heathen_aboard and not flag.crew_first_signed
cards.title: Short of the font
cards.intention: The priest of the landing says there is a way for your heathen to deal with Christians without being baptised.

options.label: Let the priest sign him, since the Dane is willing
Give the priest something for his poor and leave the Dane as he is (4 d)
He is a good hand as he is

memory.sign: had his heathen signed with the cross
memory.alms: gave alms and kept his heathen as he was
memory.no: would not have his heathen signed

cards.note: Sickness 1: the warning before the fever (BRIEF rule 6 and CHAINS.md 5: every danger warns first). Telling him to row it off sets crew_fever_risk, which brings crew.sick.fever.
cards.when: not moored and days_at_sea > 2 and health < 0.9 and not flag.crew_fever_risk
cards.title: A cough in the night
cards.intention: The hand has coughed through two watches. The mate does not like the sound of it.

options.label: Give him the dry place under the foredeck and the spare cloak
Warm a cup of the cargo's ale or mead for him over the fire-stone
Tell him to row it off

cards.note: Sickness 2 (sample 21): the fever. It comes only after the cough was ignored or when the crew's health is already low. A death leaves a body aboard (crew.death.body) and a share owed to his kin (crew.death.kin). Bleeding and prayer as the two cures: Bald's Leechbook, a 9th-century English book of cures (npc_roles_793.json leech).
cards.when: not moored and days_at_sea > 3 and (flag.crew_fever_risk or health < 0.7)
cards.title: Fever aboard
cards.intention: The hand burns and shakes and cannot row. What is done with him today decides whether he lives.

options.label: Rest him in the stern under the spare sail
Put in to the nearest shore and lie a day by a fire
Keep him at his oar: the work will sweat it out

memory.rest.failure: lost a man to fever at sea
memory.shore.failure: lost a man to fever on a strange shore
memory.oar.failure: kept a sick man at his oar until he died

cards.note: Sickness 3: in port. A leech lets blood, sets bones and gives herbs (Old English laece; Bald's Leechbook names 'lencten adl', the spring fever) (?). The woman with the knots: the Indiculus superstitionum et paganiarum (about 743) lists amulets and knots (c. 10) and incantations (c. 12) among things the Church forbids (npc_roles_793.json wise_woman).
cards.when: moored and health < 0.8
cards.title: The leech and the knots
cards.intention: The men are in poor health. A leech at the landing offers his craft; there is also a woman up the lane.

options.label: Pay the leech (3 d)
Send to the woman with the knots (1 d)
Broth, a dry floor and two days' sleep

cards.note: A death 1: what is done with the body at sea. The law quoted is the Capitulatio de partibus Saxoniae c. 22 (Munro 1900), said only while it is fresh law (before 830). After baptism Frisians lie in graves without goods round a wooden church on the mound (peoples/frisian.md 11). What seamen of 793 did with their dead far from a church is not recorded (?): the three choices are the three a small boat has. The king given to the sea is Scyld (Beowulf, fitt I).
cards.when: flag.crew_body_aboard and not moored
cards.title: The body
cards.intention: The hand is dead and lies under the spare sail. He was baptised. The nearest church is days away.

options.label: Keep him aboard and make for the nearest church
Give him to the sea: sewn in his cloak, a stone at his feet, the steersman to say the Our Father
Land on the nearest shore and lay him under stones above the tide mark

memory.church: carried a dead man to church ground
memory.sea: gave a baptised man to the sea
memory.shore: buried a man on a strange shore

cards.note: A death 2: the body brought to a landing. A priest asks who says the stranger was baptised; proof is an oath on relics (peoples/frisian.md 3). A payment at the open grave (English soul-scot) is law only later (Aethelstan, Cnut): in 793 a gift for the grave and the mass is custom (?). In a port without a church the Christian traders bury their own (Birka's and Sliaswic's Christians: Rimbert c. 11, 24) (?).
cards.when: moored and flag.crew_body_for_church
cards.title: Church ground
cards.intention: You have brought the dead hand to a landing. He must be put in the ground today.

options.label: Pay for the grave, a mass and bread for the poor in his name (6 d)
The steersman swears to his baptism, and the crew dig the grave themselves
Leave two pennies with the gravedigger and catch the tide (2 d)

memory.mass: paid for a mass for his dead hand
memory.quick: left his dead hand to the gravedigger

cards.note: A death 3: the dead man's share. His mother finds the boat in a Frankish (Frisian) port. Fifteen pennies is sixty days on the tally. A reputation deed for this does not exist yet (see the report's needs), so only her feeling and the crew's heart move.
cards.when: moored and port.realm = franks and flag.crew_dead_share_owed and not flag.crew_body_aboard and not flag.crew_body_for_church
cards.title: The dead man's share
cards.intention: The mother of the hand who died has found the boat. His share and his things are still aboard.

options.label: Pay his whole share, give her his things and tell her where he lies (15 d)
Pay the share less what his burying cost (9 d)
Give her the knife, the cloak and the comb, and promise the silver

memory.all: paid a dead man's share to his mother
memory.less: paid a dead man's share less his burying
memory.things: gave a dead man's mother his things and a promise

cards.note: A death 4: after a burial the Dane says what he wants done with himself. Burning a body 'in accordance with pagan rites' is death in the king's Saxon lands (Capitulatio de partibus Saxoniae c. 7, Munro 1900); what a Frisian count would do is not recorded (?). Heathen Northmen burn or mound their dead (peoples/norse.md 11). It records a promise only: what becomes of any named man is his own chain's.
cards.when: not moored and storm < 0.3 and (flag.crew_buried_at_sea or flag.crew_buried_church or flag.crew_buried_ashore) and (year < 816 or flag.crew_heathen_aboard) and not flag.crew_word_to_dane
cards.title: What the Dane wants done
cards.intention: Some days after the burial the Dane tells you, once, what he wants if he dies aboard.

options.label: Give him your word
No fire where the count's men can see smoke: the sea you can promise
Tell him to stay alive

memory.word: gave his word on how the Dane is to be buried
memory.sea: promised the Dane the sea and no priest

cards.note: Hunger 1: at sea. The Dane says Havamal 21 (texts_793.json havamal_021, Bellows 1923), given if the ration is halved. Rations and their goods: voyage_rules.json.
cards.when: not moored and days_at_sea > 4 and health < 0.75
cards.title: Green bread
cards.intention: The stores are nearly gone and land is days off. The mate asks how the rest is to be shared.

options.label: Half a ration each till landfall, yours with theirs
Lines over the side and the small net
Open a cheese from the cargo

cards.note: Hunger 2: at anchor off a farm. The lookout's law is Ine 20 (Wessex, about 694): a man from afar or a stranger who goes off the track and neither shouts nor blows a horn is to be taken for a thief, to be killed or redeemed (npc_text_encounters.md 1.1, the host; wording to check (?)).
cards.when: not moored and not under_way and days_at_sea > 3 and health < 0.8
cards.title: A farm above the strand
cards.intention: The men are hungry and the boat lies off a lone farm. The farmer is watching, and has sent a child running inland.

options.label: Blow the horn and walk up with silver in an open hand (6 d)
Blow the horn and offer a bundle of whetstones for bread and a sheep
Blow the horn and ask plainly for what he can spare

cards.note: Hunger 3: the spine's hook for the crew in thread hungry_years ('the men watch what the merchant does with a hold full of wheat in a hungry port; the mate has seen an army eat a district bare'). The famine of 792-794 and of 805-806; Frankfurt, June 794, c. 4: no more than 4 d for a modius of wheat, the king's own grain cheaper (chronicle_793.json 794-06-01-frankfurt-prices; spine.json hungry_years). Giving a sack sets the thread's flag hy_fed_poor; what is asked in the market is the market's own business.
cards.when: moored and port.realm = franks and hold.wheat > 0 and (year < 795 or (year >= 805 and year < 808))
cards.title: Wheat in a hungry port
cards.intention: There is famine ashore and wheat in the hold. The men are watching what you do with it.

options.label: Give a sack at the church door, through the priest
Tell the men it goes at the king's price and no more
It goes to whoever pays most: that is what a market is

memory.give: gave wheat to the poor in a famine
memory.dear: meant to sell wheat dear in a famine

cards.note: Cold 1: a winter night at sea. The mate's jibe is Notker, Gesta Karoli I.34 (tr. A. J. Grant, 1905, as quoted in peoples/frisian.md 8): Charlemagne on the short cloaks the Frisians sold at the long cloaks' price; the complaint about cloak lengths is in the king's letter to Offa of 796, so the line is said from 796. The Dane says Havamal 3 (texts_793.json havamal_003, Bellows 1923).
cards.when: not moored and (month >= 10 or month <= 3) and (hour >= 21 or hour < 5) and storm < 0.3
cards.title: Frost on the thwarts
cards.intention: A night watch in the cold months. The men are stiff, wet and a long way from a fire.

options.label: Put in to the shore and light a fire till the sky greys
Break out a bolt of the cargo's cloth for wraps: the salt may spoil it
Two at the oars, turn about, till they are warm

cards.note: Cold 2: ice in the harbour (decision 17 of 4 Oct: the river freezing some years). The Dane says a line of Havamal 81 (texts_793.json havamal_081, Bellows 1923). A sprung plank is twelve pennies at the wright's (a guess to tune).
cards.when: moored and ice > 0 and not flag.crew_hauled_out
cards.title: Ice at the piles
cards.intention: The harbour is freezing. Ice that closes on a hull can open her seams.

options.label: Hire the strand's men and their rollers and haul her out (5 d)
The crew break the ice round her every dawn
Leave her: it will thaw

cards.note: Cold 3: the lookout says the opening of The Seafarer and gives it whole (texts_793.json seafarer: Lola La Motte Iddings in Cook and Tinker, Select Translations from Old English Poetry, 1902; the two lines quoted are from that entry, whose rights note asks for a check of the translator's death year before shipping outside the US). The poem is in the Exeter Book of about 975 and may be older.
cards.when: not moored and (month >= 10 or month <= 3) and hour >= 17 and storm < 0.3 and not text.seafarer
cards.title: A true song
cards.intention: A cold evening at sea. The lookout knows an English song made by a man who had sat where he sits.

options.label: Hear it through
Say it in summer, when a man can laugh at it

cards.note: Boredom 1: becalmed. The swimming is Beowulf and Breca (fitts IX-X), named only if the fitt has been heard. The failed swim's joke is the Lex Frisionum (about 802) XXII: seizing a man by the hair costs two shillings, and pulling a man out of the water earns four (XXII.87, as numbered in peoples/frisian.md 9 and 12). Bone dice are common finds of the period (?).
cards.when: under_way and wind < 1.5 and days_at_sea > 1 and storm < 0.1 and hour >= 8 and hour <= 19
cards.title: No wind
cards.intention: Becalmed since dawn. The men have nothing to do and have begun on each other.

options.label: A swimming match round the boat, a cup of ale to the winner
Out oars: an hour's pull earns the evening ale
Let them dice for their knives

cards.note: Boredom 2: the board game. Tafl (Old English taefl): a king in the middle with his men, and twice as many attackers; boards and pieces of the 8th century and earlier are known (the board found at the monastery of Deer, a glass piece from Lindisfarne in an 8th- to 9th-century layer) (?). riddles_793.json r-gest-19 is the game's own riddle and is had elsewhere.
cards.when: not moored and storm < 0.2 and wind < 6 and days_at_sea > 1 and (year < 816 or flag.crew_heathen_aboard)
cards.title: A board on the thwart
cards.intention: The Dane has cut a board of squares into a thwart and shaken out a bag of bone pegs. He is looking for someone to play.

options.label: Sit down opposite him
Let him teach the lookout, and watch the moves
Play if you like, but no silver on the board in this boat

cards.note: Boredom 3: three wonders at anchor, each true to its teller's people. The Frisian's: the Liber Monstrorum I.2 (English, about 700) says the bones of Hygelac, king of the Geats, killed raiding the Franks, are kept on an island in the Rhine where it breaks into the Ocean and shown to travellers as a wonder; the raid is Gregory of Tours, Historiae III.3 (Chlochilaicus, about 520). The Dane's: the great fish taken for an island, on which sailors land and light a fire (the Physiologus; the Old English 'Whale' in the Exeter Book). The lookout's: the sparrow in the hall (Bede, Historia ecclesiastica II.13, 731). Our renderings. The king's bones are heard again when the song comes to his fall (crew.song.fitt_19, fitt_33).
cards.when: not moored and not under_way and hour >= 18 and storm < 0.2
cards.title: Three wonders
cards.intention: At anchor in the evening the men are telling wonders for a cup of ale. You are the judge.

options.label: The cup to the king's bones
The cup to the island that was a fish
The cup to the sparrow

cards.note: Low heart: the lookout tells Deor and gives it (texts_793.json deor: F. A. Blackburn's paraphrase in Cook and Tinker 1902, with the same rights note as the Seafarer). The refrain is rendered in our own words (Old English: thaes ofereode, thisses swa maeg). The poem is in the Exeter Book of about 975; Weland and the others are older tales.
cards.when: not moored and storm < 0.3 and heart < 0.4 and not text.deor
cards.title: That passed
cards.intention: The crew's heart is low and nobody is speaking. The lookout offers the one song he knows for it.

options.label: Hear it
Songs do not row: open a cask of the cargo's ale
A hard hour at the oars, and a plain word about where the next silver is

cards.note: A fight 1. The steersman's law is the Lex Frisionum (about 802) XXII, the schedule of hurts: seizing a man by the hair, two shillings; ducking him, four; the law prices deeds, not words, and no Frisian insult word survives (peoples/frisian.md 9: do not invent one). The Frisian shilling is three pennies in the middle district (Additio III). Comes when the heart is low or a dicing quarrel is fresh.
cards.when: not moored and (heart < 0.5 or flag.crew_quarrel) and not flag.crew_feud and not flag.crew_fight_ashore
cards.title: Blows
cards.intention: The hand and the lookout are fighting between the thwarts. The steersman has a hand on each and is waiting for you.

options.label: Part them: each pays the other's hurt from his share, as the law prices it
They finish it at the next landing: fists, no iron, the rest of you watching
One to the bow, one to the stern, and not a word

memory.price: made each pay the other's hurt
memory.strand: put the fight off to the strand
memory.apart: sent them to opposite ends of the boat

cards.note: A fight 2: settled on the strand. No ordeal or sworn duel: the duel with hired champions is East Frisian law (Lex Frisionum XIV) and is not what two hands do.
cards.when: moored and flag.crew_fight_ashore
cards.title: On the strand
cards.intention: The two who fought aboard are on the strand at the ebb to finish it. Half the landing has come down to watch.

options.label: Let them
Stop it at first blood and make them drink from one cup (1 d)
Forbid it: not in front of a town the house trades in

cards.note: A fight 3, and a man leaving: a feud aboard a boat seven paces long. Peace sworn on relics: proof and peace among Frisians and English are oaths on relics (peoples/frisian.md 3, english.md 9). The proverb in the outcome is Durham Proverbs (an 11th-century English manuscript): 'they do not quarrel who are not together' (our rendering) (?).
cards.when: moored and flag.crew_feud
cards.title: One of them goes
cards.intention: A knife was drawn in the night. The mate says the boat is too small for both men.

options.label: Pay off the hand (6 d)
Pay off the lookout (6 d)
Keep both: each swears peace on the relics here, his hand in the other's

memory.hand: paid off the hand after a knife was drawn
memory.lookout: paid off the lookout after a knife was drawn

cards.note: A theft 1: six pennies gone from the purse. Nicking silver to test and mark it is the northern habit (peoples/norse.md 5). The marked coins lead to crew.theft.caught.
cards.when: silver >= 40 and not flag.crew_theft_watch and not flag.crew_thief_known and not flag.crew_theft_warned
cards.title: Six pennies light
cards.intention: Silver is missing from the purse. There are four men aboard and no door.

options.label: Turn out every bundle now, your own first
Say nothing, nick the edge of every coin left, and watch
Tell them the next loss comes out of every share alike

cards.note: A theft 2: the thief found. Theft paid back twofold with the peace-money (freda) to the king is the Frisian law's shape (Lex Frisionum III) (?); a master's justice on his own boat is not written anywhere.
cards.when: flag.crew_theft_watch or flag.crew_thief_known
cards.title: The nicked penny
cards.intention: The missing silver has been traced to the hand. He does not deny it.

options.label: Put him ashore at the next landing with what he is owed, less the six
He pays it back twice over from his share, and keeps his oar
Ask what the debt is, and lend him the six against his season's share

memory.twice: made a thief pay twice over
memory.lend.success: lent a thief the silver he had stolen

cards.note: A friendship 1: the hand and the Dane. The Dane says Havamal 47 (texts_793.json havamal_047, Bellows 1923), given if they are put on one watch. Bonds between peoples aboard: Plans/crew.md C4.
cards.when: not moored and storm < 0.3 and days_at_sea > 2 and (flag.crew_friends or heart >= 0.7) and (year < 816 or flag.crew_heathen_aboard)
cards.title: One cloak
cards.intention: The hand and the Dane have become friends. It changes how the watches fall.

options.label: Put them on one watch for the season
Advance them three pennies between them for the net they want (3 d)
Keep them on separate watches: friends talk more than they pull

cards.note: A friendship 2: a gift looks for a gift. Havamal 41 (texts_793.json havamal_041, Bellows 1923) is given with the comb; 'a gift asks a gift': peoples/norse.md 5. A beast biting its own back is the northern ornament of the late 8th century (?). A dozen antler combs is 12 d in goods_793.json, so one is a penny.
cards.when: flag.crew_friends and (year < 816 or flag.crew_heathen_aboard)
cards.title: A gift looks for a gift
cards.intention: The Dane has given the hand a thing he made. The hand has nothing to give back, and comes to you.

options.label: Advance him four pennies on his share (4 d)
Let him have one antler comb from the cargo, on his tally (1 d)
Tell him a gift owed is no shame before Yule

cards.note: Teaching a tongue 1: the Dane's. Old Frisian and Old Norse count nearly alike and part company soon after (the game's kin table: 0.35, npc_text_encounters.md 2.6). The lesson lifts the merchant's Norse to a half; 'tongue' does nothing in the game yet (GameEffects.Tongue), so the flag crew_norse_1 carries the progress meanwhile.
cards.when: not moored and storm < 0.3 and days_at_sea > 1 and not flag.crew_norse_1 and (year < 816 or flag.crew_heathen_aboard)
cards.title: Counting in Danish
cards.intention: The Dane is teaching the hand his tongue, a word to each stroke of the oar. You could learn it with him.

options.label: Take the oar beside them and learn it too
Let them be: a hand who can ask a price in the north is worth his bread
Tell them to count in their heads

cards.note: Teaching a tongue 2: the second lesson, a voyage or more later. The hall door's greeting is Havamal 2 (texts_793.json havamal_002, Bellows 1923). Sliesthorp is the Danes' market on the Schlei (ports_793.json sliesthorp).
cards.when: not moored and storm < 0.3 and days_at_sea > 2 and flag.crew_norse_1 and not flag.crew_norse_2 and (year < 816 or flag.crew_heathen_aboard)
cards.title: How to refuse in Danish
cards.intention: You can count and ask a price in the Dane's tongue. He offers the next lesson.

options.label: Learn the market words
Ask instead for what a guest says at a hall door
Enough for one voyage

cards.note: Teaching a tongue 3: Frisian and English. The two are near kin (the game's kin table: 0.5; how near in speech is not recorded: peoples/frisian.md 10) (?). The law the lookout gives is Hlothhere and Eadric 16 (Kent, 673-685): a Kentishman buying in Lundenwic is to have two or three true men to witness, or the king's wic-reeve (as quoted in peoples/english.md 8).
cards.when: not moored and storm < 0.3 and days_at_sea > 1 and not flag.crew_english_1
cards.title: Bread, butter and cheese
cards.intention: The English lookout and the Frisian steersman have found how near their tongues lie. It is a thing a merchant can use.

options.label: Have the lookout give you the English for every thing in the hold
Ask him what an English reeve says when a foreign boat lands
Leave them to it

cards.note: Teaching a tongue 4: letters. A waxed tablet and a pointed stylus are the schoolroom's tools (riddles_793.json riddle_aldhelm_32_pugillares); the Latin row has twenty-three letters. The mate's line touches his own want (the spine: he thinks reading is how his brother will be found) and goes no further. Reading comes by 'learn latin'.
cards.when: not moored and storm < 0.2 and wind < 6 and not learned.latin and not flag.crew_letters_1
cards.title: Twenty-three marks
cards.intention: The lookout is showing the mate his letters on a waxed board. There is room on the thwart for a third.

options.label: Sit down by the mate and learn them too
Have him cut your own name and the boat's
Leave them to it

cards.note: Teaching a tongue 5: runes. The Northmen's row has sixteen staves by about 800, cut down from the older twenty-four (peoples/norse.md 13: they use 16; npc_text_encounters.md 1.4); the staves named are fe (cattle, wealth), ass (the god) and iss (ice) (?). Reading comes by 'learn runes'.
cards.when: not moored and storm < 0.2 and wind < 6 and not learned.runes and not flag.crew_runes_1 and (year < 816 or flag.crew_heathen_aboard)
cards.title: Sixteen staves
cards.intention: The Dane is cutting his people's letters into the edge of a thwart with his knife.

options.label: Have him say each one, and cut them yourself beside his
Have him cut the boat's name where the toll man will not look
Tell him to cut his lessons on a stick, not on the boat

cards.note: Riddles for sport 1: fog. Gestumblindi's riddle 5 (riddles_793.json r-gest-05: 'given, at sea', a seaman's riddle; text t-gest-05, Vigfusson and Powell, Corpus Poeticum Boreale, 1883). The saga that holds it is 13th-century, the riddles older (toldLater). The Dane never gives an answer, only the next question (the spine, thread riddle_road).
cards.when: not moored and fog >= 0.6 and not riddle.r-gest-05 and (year < 816 or flag.crew_heathen_aboard)
cards.title: A riddle in the fog
cards.intention: Fog, and nothing to do but listen. The Dane asks a riddle to keep the men from hearing things.

options.label: Take the riddle
Tell him to listen for surf

cards.note: Riddles for sport 2: dew. Gestumblindi's riddle 3 (riddles_793.json r-gest-03: 'given, at sea: seamen pass riddles to while away the watch'; text t-gest-03, Corpus Poeticum Boreale, 1883).
cards.when: not moored and not under_way and hour >= 4 and hour <= 6 and storm < 0.2 and not riddle.r-gest-03 and (year < 816 or flag.crew_heathen_aboard)
cards.title: A riddle at dawn
cards.intention: Dawn at anchor. Everything aboard is wet and it has not rained. The Dane has a riddle for it.

options.label: Take the riddle
Not before bread

cards.note: Riddles for sport 3: the anchor. Exeter Book riddle 16 (riddles_793.json riddle_exeter_16_anchor: 'given, at sea: ship's gear is every seaman's riddle'; text exeter_16_anchor, Benjamin Thorpe, Codex Exoniensis, 1842). The manuscript is of about 970; such riddles were made by English monks from Aldhelm's day (d. 709). The indecent ones: the onion and the key (peoples/english.md 9).
cards.when: not moored and not under_way and storm < 0.3 and not riddle.riddle_exeter_16_anchor
cards.title: A riddle at anchor
cards.intention: The boat lies to her anchor and the lookout remembers a riddle the monks made.

options.label: Take the riddle
Ask whether the monks made any that were less holy

cards.note: Riddles for sport 4: hail and rain. Gestumblindi's riddle 10 (riddles_793.json r-gest-10: 'given, at sea: weather lore passes between seamen'; text t-gest-10, Corpus Poeticum Boreale, 1883).
cards.when: not moored and storm >= 0.3 and storm < 0.6 and not riddle.r-gest-10 and (year < 816 or flag.crew_heathen_aboard)
cards.title: A riddle after the squall
cards.intention: A squall has gone through and left hail in the bilge. The Dane has a riddle for that too.

options.label: Take the riddle
Bail first

cards.note: Riddles for sport 5: where the wind comes from. Vafthruthnir's lay, stanza 36 (riddles_793.json r-vafth-36: 'given, at sea'; text t-vafth-36, H. A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, 1923). Written down about 1270, older in substance (toldLater); the contest in which the asker stakes his head is the lay's own frame.
cards.when: under_way and wind >= 8 and storm < 0.3 and not riddle.r-vafth-36 and (year < 816 or flag.crew_heathen_aboard)
cards.title: A riddle on a fair wind
cards.intention: She is running well. The Dane asks where the thing that drives her comes from.

options.label: Take the riddle
From the south-west: ask the sail

cards.note: Riddles for sport 6: the names of the calm. Alvis's lay, stanza 22 (riddles_793.json r-alv-22: 'given, at sea', from 860 in the table; text t-alv-22, Bellows 1923). For the later crews: only from 860 and only with a heathen hand aboard.
cards.when: under_way and wind < 1.5 and storm < 0.1 and year >= 860 and flag.crew_heathen_aboard and not riddle.r-alv-22
cards.title: A riddle with no wind in it
cards.intention: Becalmed. The Dane gives five names for one thing and asks what men call it.

options.label: Take the riddle
I call it a day's pay gone

cards.note: Riddles for sport 7: the answer brought back to the setter (npc_text_encounters.md 2.9: worth 'won_riddle' and his feeling +10). Setting one back is sample 24's third option. At sea the deed has no port to count at; in a port it counts there.
cards.when: (riddle.r-gest-05 = solved or riddle.r-gest-03 = solved or riddle.r-gest-10 = solved or riddle.r-vafth-36 = solved or riddle.r-alv-22 = solved) and not flag.crew_riddle_answered and (year < 816 or flag.crew_heathen_aboard)
cards.title: The answer
cards.intention: You have the answer to one of the Dane's riddles. He has been waiting to see how long it would take.

options.label: Give him your answer
Answer, and set him one of your own

memory.back.success: answered his riddle and set one he could not

cards.note: Reading with the crew 1 (sample 23; the spine's hook for the crew in riddle_road): the Dane reads a rune stick in part and the merchant finishes it. One stave stands for several sounds in the sixteen-rune row (npc_text_encounters.md 1.4). 'chest.rune_count' reads 0 until the chest counts rune texts, so the card waits for that.
cards.when: not moored and storm < 0.2 and chest.rune_count > 0 and not learned.runes and (year < 816 or flag.crew_heathen_aboard)
cards.title: A rune stick
cards.intention: There is a rune-cut stick in the chest that you cannot read. The Dane can, and will do some of it.

options.label: Let him read his part, and work out the rest
Ask him to read all of it
Read it yourself, stave by stave

cards.note: Reading with the crew 2 (sample 23 and 15; the spine's hook in riddle_road): the lookout, schooled as a boy by monks, reads a Latin leaf slowly and in part. Few merchants read Latin (npc_text_encounters.md 1.4).
cards.when: not moored and storm < 0.2 and chest.latin_count > 0 and not learned.latin
cards.title: A Latin leaf
cards.intention: There is a leaf of Latin in the chest that you cannot read. The lookout can read some of it.

options.label: Have him read what he can, and puzzle out the rest with him
Ask him only to tell you what it says
Put it back in the chest till a monk is aboard

cards.note: A new hand 1: a younger son of the terp country, whose brother has the farm (land reckoned in cattle, inherited: peoples/frisian.md 2-3). A boy's wage of half a man's is a guess (?). Hired from the port's own people: Plans/crew.md C3.
cards.when: moored and port.realm = franks and (crew < 4 or flag.crew_short_handed)
cards.title: A boy by the mooring post
cards.intention: The boat is a man short. A farmer's younger son asks for the empty oar.

options.label: Take him at a boy's wage till Martinmas
Take him at a man's wage from the first day, with hand-money (2 d)
Tell him to come back with a beard

memory.man: took him on at a man's wage when he was a boy

cards.note: A new hand 2: a Dane left behind by his ship. Danes came to Dorestad to trade (Rimbert c. 24; peoples/frisian.md 10). Before 800 the steersman speaks of Lindisfarne (8 June 793: chronicle_793.json); from 830 a priest may sign a heathen with the cross short of baptism (Rimbert c. 24). Hiring him sets crew_heathen_aboard, which the Dane's cards ask for after the first crew's years.
cards.when: moored and (crew < 4 or flag.crew_short_handed) and not flag.crew_heathen_aboard and year >= 794
cards.title: A Dane mending nets
cards.intention: The boat is a man short. A Dane whose ship went home without him is looking for an oar.

options.label: Hire him
Hire him if he will let a priest sign him with the cross first
Not this season

cards.note: A man leaving 1: another master offers the hand better. A penny every three days against the house's penny every four (voyage_rules.json); meat twice a week is a guess (?). A man paid off goes to that port's pool and may be met again (npc_text_encounters.md 2.5).
cards.when: moored and port.kind = emporium and crew >= 4 and heart < 0.7
cards.title: Twelve oars for the Seine
cards.intention: The master of a bigger ship wants your hand, and says so in front of you.

options.label: Match it (8 d)
Let him go, paid to the day, and shake the skipper's hand (6 d)
Hold him to his word till Martinmas

memory.bless: let his hand go to a better ship with good grace
memory.word.failure: held a man to his word, who went anyway

cards.note: A man leaving 2: a hand marries ashore. A widow holds her dead husband's house and gives land in her own name (peoples/frisian.md 3: Diethilt; a widow rules her son's house, Vita Liudgeri I.6). A bolt of Frisian cloth is 48 d in goods_793.json: a rich gift. A share in place of a wage as in crew.pay.wage_or_share.
cards.when: moored and port.realm = franks and crew >= 3 and not flag.crew_man_went_home
cards.title: A roof that wants a man
cards.intention: The hand is leaving the sea to marry a widow with a boat-shed. He is telling you, not asking.

options.label: Pay him to the day, and a bolt of good cloth for the bride (6 d)
Pay him to the day and wish him cows (6 d)
Ask him for one more season, at a share and not a wage

memory.gift: gave cloth for his bride when he left the boat
memory.pay: paid him off fairly when he married

cards.note: Winter ashore 1: the boat hauled and mended. Nobody sails in winter (peoples/norse.md 6); winter is 'men at nets and hulls' (peoples/frisian.md 2). Clinker seams are packed with tarred wool, hair or moss (?). Tar: goods_793.json (a barrel 20 d; a small boat takes a tenth of one).
cards.when: moored and (month = 11 or month = 12) and not flag.crew_boat_tarred
cards.title: Up the strand
cards.intention: The season is over. The boat comes out of the water, and the steersman wants her seams done while she is dry.

options.label: Haul her and do it now: tar, moss and the strand's men (8 d)
Haul her and broach the tar in the hold (3 d for moss and rollers)
Haul her, and leave the tar till spring

cards.note: Winter ashore 2: where four men sleep till spring. A host answers for the strangers he lodges (npc_roles_793.json host; Hlothhere and Eadric 15) (?); a shipmaster winters as a guest (peoples/norse.md 5). The Dane says Havamal 35 (texts_793.json havamal_035, Bellows 1923). Candlemas is 2 February. Sixteen pennies is four men at a penny a week for the dark quarter.
cards.when: moored and (month = 12 or month = 1) and not flag.crew_winter_lodged
cards.title: Four men and three months of dark
cards.intention: The boat is laid up. The men must sleep and eat somewhere until the sea opens.

options.label: The host's fire till Candlemas (16 d)
The boat-shed and a fire-pit (4 d)
Send each man to his own hearth till the geese go north

cards.note: Winter ashore 3: idle hands. Hemp to rope: goods_793.json (a bundle 5 d, a coil 10 d). Letters by the fire: 'learn latin' (a monastery winter is one of the ways to Latin, npc_text_encounters.md 2.6). The ninth hour is mid-afternoon by the Church's reckoning.
cards.when: moored and (month = 12 or month = 1 or month = 2)
cards.title: Long nights
cards.intention: Midwinter ashore. The men have nothing to do, and the mate wants them given something.

options.label: Set them to lay rope from the hemp in the hold
Let the lookout teach letters by the fire to whoever will sit
Stand them an evening at the ale-house and say nothing of work (3 d)

cards.note: Winter ashore 4: Christmas and Yule. Bede, De temporum ratione c. 15 (725): the heathen English began their year on 25 December, the night 'we hold so sacred', which they called Modranecht, the mothers' night; the lookout was schooled in Bede's house. A king 'drinking Yule' at sea: Haraldskvaedi, about 900 (peoples/norse.md 4). Comes on Christmas Eve and Christmas Day (Feasts.On).
cards.when: moored and month = 12 and feast and (year < 816 or flag.crew_heathen_aboard)
cards.title: Midwinter
cards.intention: Christmas. The church is full. The Dane has a fire of his own behind the boat-shed and has asked nobody.

options.label: Mass with the Christians, then the Dane's fire with all of them (3 d for ale)
Mass, and the host's table after
Go and sit at his fire now

cards.note: Winter ashore 5: the muster in spring, if the men were sent home (crew.winter.lodging). Hand-money to bind a hiring is a guess (?).
cards.when: moored and flag.crew_scattered and month >= 3 and month <= 4
cards.title: Three men by the boat
cards.intention: The sea is opening. Of the men sent home for the winter, one has not come back.

options.label: Wait a week for him
Send his cousin back with hand-money and a day named (2 d)
Sail a man short and hire at the first landing

cards.note: The spine's hook for the crew in thread silver_road: the Dane tests silver with a knife and trusts no stamp; the steersman trusts the king's penny and nothing else; the first time the purse holds three kinds of silver they argue about what the boat is worth. The purse starts with deniers, English pennies, dirhams and hacksilver (trade_rules.json start). North of the Eider silver goes by weight, nicked and tested (peoples/norse.md 5). Sets none of the thread's sv_ flags.
cards.when: not moored and storm < 0.3 and silver >= 60 and year < 830
cards.title: Three kinds of silver
cards.intention: The purse is tipped out to be counted. The Dane and the steersman do not agree on what is in it.

options.label: Reckon it the Dane's way: all of it by weight
Reckon it the steersman's way: the king's penny, and the rest at what a moneyer gives
Reckon it both ways and believe the smaller

cards.note: The spine's hook for the crew in thread swords_north: the Dane knows who buys and says the Franks made the law because they fear the edge; the steersman will not row a cargo that can hang him; the mate would arm anyone the king calls an enemy. The law: no mail coats out of the realm (Herstal 779); no arms to the Slavs and Avars but by the king's posts (Thionville 805); arms to the Northmen on pain of death (Pitres 864): trade_rules.json laws. Sets none of the thread's sw_ flags.
cards.when: not moored and hold.weapons > 0 and year < 901
cards.title: Iron under the ballast
cards.intention: There are blades in the hold that the king's law forbids. The steersman wants it said aloud.

options.label: A double share this voyage for every man, for the risk (12 d)
Give your word that this is the last such cargo
Tell him his work is the steering oar

memory.last: gave his word to carry no more blades
memory.steer: told him to steer and not to ask

cards.note: The spine's hook for the crew in thread book_road: the lookout can read a book aloud at anchor, and wants to; a wet book is a ruined book; where it rides in a seven-metre boat is a real question (sets bk_lost if it goes wrong). A book is 360 d in goods_793.json. Waxed cloth: Saint Cuthbert's body was wrapped in a waxed cloth in 698 (?). Each option's odds show as a word before it is chosen.
cards.when: not moored and storm < 0.3 and hold.books > 0 and year < 876
cards.title: Where the book rides
cards.intention: There is a book in the cargo. The lookout says there is no dry place aboard, and asks to read from it.

options.label: It rides in his sea-chest, wrapped in waxed cloth, and stays shut
It rides in his chest, and he may read aloud from it at anchor
Under the stern boards with the silver

memory.read.success: let him read from a book at anchor

cards.note: The spine's hook for the crew in thread godfreds_market: the Dane knows men in that fleet and says less than he means; the steersman's kin are on the islands. cards.note: THE EVENING SONG, 1 of 43 (research_indie_and_concept.md 4.5: one of the four knows a song by heart and gives a fitt of Beowulf each evening at sea). Each card gives one fitt (texts_793.json beowulf_01 to beowulf_43: Old English after Harrison and Sharp 1894, English by J. L. Hall 1892, the fitts numbered as Hall has them) and asks for the fitt before it, so they come in order, one an evening (the flag crew_song_tonight lapses in 0.6 of a day). The lookout tells it in his own plain words first; the fitt itself is the chest's text. No music is needed: he says it (the user set music aside, 4 Oct 2026). The poem's manuscript is of about 1000 and the poem older by an unknown span (?).
